extracted.intended_audience: OSHA stakeholders and commenters, regulatory analysts, economists, small business representatives, and other parties responding to the NPRM
extracted.subtask_short: OSHA NPRM benefits and IRFA guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the evaluative criteria and analytic assumptions OSHA used in the proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard's benefits analysis and the statutory elements required for the Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA). Useful for commenters and analysts reviewing OSHA's economic and regulatory analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underreporting of Heat-Related Fatalities
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA preliminarily determined that there is reason to believe that the number of heat-related fatalities in CFOI are undercounted and, for this analysis, estimates that occupational fatalities due to heat are undercounted by a factor of 14.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: comparison of excess-deaths studies (e.g., Weinberger et al., 2020) and death-certificate based counts (e.g., Xu, Fowler et al.) suggests national undercounting (13.7–14.6 fold); however, it is unclear what proportion of excess deaths were among workers. OSHA did not adjust the ratio further because of uncertainty about work-related share. OSHA presents alternative undercount factors in sensitivity analysis (e.g., 3X, 14X, 15X) and welcomes comment and additional studies or alternative underreporting factors to refine this estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underreporting of Non-Fatal Heat-Related Injuries (HRIs)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA estimates that HRIs are undercounted by a factor of 7.5 (midpoint of 5 and 10) based on available studies comparing BLS SOII to other data sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: Joe et al. (2014) found State-based sources contained 5–10 times more certain injuries than SOII; Heinzerling et al. (2020) found 3–6 times more HRI claims in California workers' compensation versus SOII. Caveats: methodological differences, incomplete capture in comparison datasets, and case-matching limitations. OSHA uses 7.5X in the primary estimate, presents other multipliers (no adjustment, 2X, 10X) in sensitivity analysis, and requests comment and additional data or methodologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of Underreporting Adjustments in Benefits Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA applies underreporting adjustment factors to BLS-reported counts to obtain underreporting-adjusted totals used in benefits calculations (e.g., applying 7.5X to BLS-reported 39,450 HRIs and 14X to 479 fatalities yields adjusted totals used in subsequent calculations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Applying factors 7.5 and 14 to BLS data produced estimated totals of 295,875 HRIs and 6,706 fatalities for 2011–2022 (annual averages). OSHA then applies program effectiveness assumptions to these adjusted totals to estimate prevented cases. Alternative underreporting assumptions are incorporated into sensitivity tables (Tables VIII.E.6–VIII.E.8). OSHA invites comment on this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program Effectiveness Assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: For the primary benefits analysis OSHA assumes the proposed standard would reduce heat-related fatalities by 95% and HRIs by 65%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity bounds: low estimate uses 90% effectiveness for fatalities and 50% for HRIs; high estimate assumes 100% effectiveness for both. Rationale/caveats: literature on intervention effectiveness is uncertain, many studies lack concurrent control groups and are industry- or setting-specific; no study exactly matches the proposed standard's controls. OSHA discusses specific study findings (e.g., McCarthy et al., 2019) but chooses conservative primary assumptions and models alternatives in sensitivity analysis to reflect uncertainty. OSHA welcomes comment on effectiveness assumptions and related evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization Inputs: Value of Statistical Life (VSL) and Value of Statistical Injury (VSI)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA uses a VSL of $13.77 million (DOT 2022 estimate converted to 2023 dollars using the GDP deflator) and a VSI of $116,588 per injury (midpoint from Viscusi and Gentry (2015), converted to 2023 dollars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These monetary inputs are applied to the estimated number of prevented fatalities and injuries (after underreporting adjustment and effectiveness assumptions) to compute monetized benefits. OSHA cites conversion methodology and specific sources (DOT, BEA GDP deflator, Viscusi & Gentry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity Analysis on Underreporting and Program Effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA performs sensitivity analyses that vary underreporting assumptions (e.g., no underreporting, 2X, 7.5X, 10X for HRIs; 3X, 14X, 15X for fatalities) and program effectiveness (low, primary, high effectiveness scenarios) to show ranges of prevented cases and monetized benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results are presented in Tables VIII.E.6–VIII.E.8 showing cases and monetized benefits for combinations of underreporting and effectiveness. Examples: primary estimate (65% HRI, 95% fatality) with OSHA primary underreporting yields $9.179 billion annual benefits; low/high effectiveness rows show alternate totals. Sensitivity analysis is used to illustrate uncertainty and potential variation in benefits estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of Indirect and Additional Unquantified Benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA recognizes additional potential benefits not included in the monetized primary estimate: avoided indirect heat-related fatalities and non-fatal injuries, increased labor supply, and reduced worker disutility from heat exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence/examples: studies linking hot temperatures to traumatic injuries (Park et al., 2021; Spector et al., 2016, etc.) suggest many heat-related injuries are not coded as such; illustrative calculation: if direct+indirect HRIs are as high as 72,000 annually and 65% are prevented, an additional ~47,000 prevented injuries could add ~$5.5 billion. Worker WTP estimates and possible productivity/labor-supply gains are discussed (e.g., WTP $2.60–$4.60/day; $3/day example yielding $3.236 billion). OSHA does not incorporate these in the main quantified estimate due to uncertainty but notes they may increase benefits and invites comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and Limitations of Excess-Death (Epidemiological) Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA discusses that ICD/death-certificate approaches undercapture heat as a cause of death and that epidemiological excess-death analyses estimate many more heat-attributable deaths; however, application of these excess-death ratios to occupational fatalities is uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA cites Weinberger et al. (2020) and other studies showing large differences between excess-deaths estimates and death-certificate counts, notes methodological differences across studies (exposure metrics, observational weather data, age groups, underlying populations), and explains why applying national excess-death multipliers directly to CFOI occupational fatalities is not straightforward. OSHA therefore uses the epidemiological evidence as a basis for underreporting adjustment while acknowledging large uncertainty and presenting alternatives in sensitivity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invitation for Public Comment on Estimates, Underreporting Adjustments, Data Sources, and Methodologies
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA explicitly welcomes comment on the estimates of avoided fatalities, the underreporting adjustment, data sources, and methodologies employed in the analysis and requests additional studies OSHA should consider and alternative underreporting factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This solicitation applies to all key analytic assumptions (undercount factors, effectiveness, monetization inputs, inclusion of indirect benefits, etc.). OSHA uses this to indicate openness to revise assumptions in the final economic analysis based on public input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (IRFA) Required Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the RFA, when an agency cannot certify no significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, the IRFA must include: (1) reasons why agency action is being considered; (2) succinct statement of objectives and legal basis; (3) description and estimate of number of small entities affected; (4) description of projected reporting, recordkeeping, and compliance requirements including classes of small entities and necessary professional skills; (5) identification of relevant Federal rules that may duplicate, overlap, or conflict; and (6) description/discussion of significant alternatives that minimize impacts (including differing compliance/reporting requirements/timetables, simplification, performance vs. design standards, or exemptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA cites statutory authority (5 U.S.C. 601 et seq., as amended) and explains that the IRFA elements may be performed in conjunction with other required analyses if they satisfy IRFA provisions. Sub-elements for alternatives explicitly include (a) differing compliance/reporting requirements or timetables; (b) clarification/consolidation/simplification; (c) performance rather than design standards; and (d) exemptions from coverage. OSHA uses this as the checklist for what the IRFA must address in the NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Screening Test for Small Entities / Certification Consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether OSHA can certify that the proposed rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, OSHA developed a screening test (similar in concept to the revenue test used elsewhere) applied to small entities (small business concerns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA states it is not able to certify that the proposed rule will not result in significant impacts on a substantial number of small entities, thus an IRFA is required. The screening test identifies minimum threshold effects on small entities and is similar to tests used elsewhere in the agency's economic analysis (see Section VIII.D.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of Uncertainty in Benefits Estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA identifies key sources of uncertainty affecting benefits estimates: potential underreporting of HRIs and fatalities, uncertainty in effectiveness of required interventions, and uncertainty in productivity/labor-supply effects recoverable via rest breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA discusses how these uncertainties affect central estimates and are examined via sensitivity analysis. Examples: underreporting multipliers might plausibly be higher (e.g., 10X vs. 7.5X for HRIs) leading to materially larger benefits; effectiveness assumptions may under- or over-estimate real-world prevention rates; productivity recuperation estimates depend on heterogeneous literature and break policies. OSHA quantifies some alternate scenarios to show impact on monetized benefits and requests comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation and Presentation of Monetized Benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA computes monetized benefits by applying underreporting adjustments to BLS counts, applying program effectiveness assumptions, and multiplying prevented fatalities/injuries by VSL and VSI respectively to get annualized monetized benefits (example primary estimate = $9.179 billion per year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA documents intermediate numbers (e.g., estimated prevented fatalities = 531/year; prevented HRIs = 16,027/year under primary assumptions), shows resulting monetized benefits separately for fatalities ($7.310 billion) and HRIs ($1.869 billion), and presents total and scenario-specific monetized benefits in Tables VIII.E.6–VIII.E.8. The methodology and conversions (GDP deflator) are cited and alternative scenarios are tabulated for transparency.
